subject: knight
pitch: A fantasy knight in battle-worn plate armour. A great helm with a narrow eye slit and a tall crimson plume, layered shoulder plates etched with gold filigree, a deep-blue surcoat with a silver griffin emblem, a tall kite shield bearing the same griffin, and a broadsword. Dents and scratches tell of many battles, and a torn crimson cape hangs from the shoulders.
reasoning:
I'm planning a fantasy knight model built with the agentic-3js-builder SDK, aiming for realistic human proportions—around 1.9 meters tall including helm and plume—as a single TypeScript module that needs to run correctly without testing.

For the stylized details, I'm thinking through how to achieve gold filigree and griffin emblems via paint or texture, battle damage via noise, and especially the torn crimson cape—likely using a membrane stretched between a shoulder edge and a jagged hem edge to get that ragged cloth look.

Actually, extruding a jagged outline in a vertical plane behind the torso might be simpler to control than membrane lerping, so I'm working out the default orientation and normal direction for that extrude to make sure the cape sits correctly behind the shoulders.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure: pelvis root, spine/chest, neck and head, paired arm and leg chains with shoulder-elbow-wrist and hip-knee-ankle joints, plus a helm fixed to the head with a plume attachment and a sword to place.

I'm deciding on a neutral standing pose with the shield arm on the left slightly forward and sword hand on the right hanging down, aiming for a readable stance roughly 1.85 m tall. I'm now working out the vertical placement of each joint along the y-axis from feet to the top of the helm plume, with the knight facing +Z and left side toward +X.

I'm fleshing out the horizontal offsets for shoulders and hips, plus limb lengths for arms and legs, and now setting up the builder configuration with a 2048-pixel paint resolution for fine surface detail. I'm also planning out the joint hierarchy, making sure each joint explicitly specifies its parent for clarity and that joint names follow the required naming pattern.

I'm manually defining the pelvis, chest, neck, and head joints with explicit positions and parent relationships rather than using an automated spine chain, so I have precise control over placement, and I'm deciding to bind body parts to specific bones explicitly for rigidity instead of relying on nearest-joint weighting.

For the legs, I'm setting up hip, knee, and ankle joints per side using a chain helper, working through how the polyline's named joints map to span positions so the tip ends up correctly placed at the ankle.

For the plate armour look, I'm weighing sweeping each limb as a smooth chain versus building rigid segmented pieces per bone — rigid segments with rounded joint caps feel more like stylized puppet armour, though I need to check the caps don't look too bulbous at the joints.

That blocky, segmented look is actually right for a primitive-built puppet, so box or low-poly sections work well for the armor pieces.

Now I'm working out the great helm: a lathed profile with a flat-ish dome top and low segment count (around 8-10) to keep that faceted, octagonal cylinder look, with a dark recessed eye slit cut into the steel-grey surface.

I'm placing the eye slit as a thin dark box embedded into the front of the helm's curved surface, computing the lathe radius at that height so it sits flush rather than floating. I'm also considering whether to add small breath-hole dots via a paint function tied to the helm's surface coordinates, though that may be overkill compared to just placing explicit small dark boxes.

Chart count per painted mesh could get large with axis-grouped faces, but shelf packing into a 2048 sheet with density scaling should handle it, as long as I keep parts under 1000, triangles under 60k, and flat colors under 64. For gold filigree detail, I'm considering a swirl or stripe pattern using sine/cosine functions of position to create line-like patterns on shoulder plates.

For the griffin emblem, I'm leaning toward using a decal rather than a plane texture, since decals conform to the curved surface of the surcoat or shield by projecting the texture along triangles near a target point and direction, avoiding the floating-texture problem a flat plane would have.

I need to use alphaTest cutout so the transparent svg background doesn't render as a solid square, and keep the emblem's own colors (silvery fills, dark outlines) rather than relying on tint. Now I'm sketching a simplified heraldic griffin silhouette in SVG paths -- body, beaked head, wings, legs, tail -- stylized enough to be recognizable without being overly detailed.

For the shield itself, I'm thinking through how to build it as an extruded kite shape (flat top, pointed bottom) and how to position and orient it in front of the character's left arm, facing forward with a slight tilt so the decal reads correctly on its face.

Working out the kite-shield geometry: rotating it about the Y-axis so its face angles outward-forward, then defining the kite outline as a set of local points extruded with a slight bevel for a blocky, low-poly look. I'm also planning a decal placement on the shield's front face, positioning it just off the surface in local coordinates.

The decal rays cast from the front against the shield's flat face, hitting the target mesh built from the surface geometry with proper UVs for the texture. For the surcoat, I'm thinking of it as a deep-blue cloth tabard draped over the torso front and back, hanging to the hips with a gap at the sides.

I'm leaning toward building the surcoat with a loft that sweeps stations from waist to hem, flaring outward, using a box-style section for a faceted stylized look and a deep-blue fill color, with the silver griffin emblem placed on the chest and gold-filigree pauldrons layered over the shoulders. Underneath, I'll add a steel breastplate beneath the surcoat for the torso structure.

Working out the loft's frame orientation to figure out which local axis actually points forward so the griffin decal lands on the front surface correctly.

Using a box section for the loft gives the torso a stylized blocky, faceted look since it's flat-shaded by default. But I need to think about rigging—since the catmull path has no weights, the whole torso would bind rigidly to whatever joint is nearest the path's start unless I explicitly pass a `bone` list spanning pelvis, chest, and neck so it deforms properly across those joints.

I'm weighing whether to go with a smooth multi-joint bone list (pelvis to chest) versus just rigidly binding the torso to a single joint like "chest," since the torso barely bends anyway and a single rigid bone reference simplifies things and avoids edge cases with span filtering near the neck.

For the surcoat I'm thinking deep blue with dirt darkening near the hem and battle scuffs using a mottled paint pattern. Then I'm building out the full palette: steel, dark steel, gold filigree, silver griffin, deep blue, crimson cape/plume, leather, dark slit, and sword/boot colors, plus a way to render battle damage as dents and scratches via noise-based darkening functions.

I'm figuring out how to compose the paint functions so each part can layer scratches, dents, and base colors together, then mapping out the overall part structure and making sure the TypeScript syntax matches what the runtime environment expects.

Sketching the module scaffold: importing THREE alongside the builder SDK's helper functions, exporting a meta object with name and description, and setting up a knight-building function that creates the builder instance and returns its root node. I'm double-checking which exports actually exist on the SDK so I use the right names for things like noise, patches, and baking utilities.

Now I'm mapping out the skeleton joints for the knight, starting with the pelvis as the root at roughly chest height and building the chest and limbs as children off that hierarchy.

I'm continuing up through the neck and head joints, placing the helm so its bottom sits near the neck and figuring out a reasonable head joint height, before moving down to the shoulders and arm chains with elbow and wrist positions calculated so the arm hangs naturally and the forearm bends forward to hold a shield.

Now I'm working out the shield's placement, angling it about 20 degrees so its face normal points slightly outward and forward, then checking that its corner positions don't awkwardly cross the body's midline given the arm's position.

Checking the math, the hand actually ends up slightly behind the shield's plane, which works fine visually since it reads as gripping the shield from behind, concealing the forearm. Now I'm laying out the leg joint hierarchy—hips, knees, ankles—symmetric across both sides using mirrored X coordinates, then moving on to define the right arm chain.

For the sword arm, I'm placing the shoulder, elbow, wrist, and hand joints, then working out the sword's orientation—planted point-down with the tip just touching the floor in a classic grounded pose, checking the blade length and angle stay proportional to a broadsword while keeping the tip at ground level.

For the cape, I'm positioning it hanging behind the shoulders down to a torn hem, setting its plane slightly behind the torso's back curve, matching its width to the shoulder span, and giving the bottom edge jagged tatters for a battle-worn look.

I'll attach the cape to the chest bone so it hangs and bends naturally with the torso, keeping the outline relative to that anchor point. The cape surface only needs to look right from behind and the sides, so I'll move on to designing the gorget—a short loft or lathe piece bridging the neck between the chest and the base of the helm.

Now I'm working out the great helm as a lathed solid of revolution around the head bone, defining a radius/height profile that tapers from a wide base near the gorget up to a rounded crown, with the closed loop of points forming the surface automatically.

I'm reasoning through whether revolving this closed profile polygon actually produces a closed surface, since the boundary only touches the axis at one point while the rest forms a diagonal edge and the main path—working out if that still sweeps into a fully enclosed solid.

Since R stays in x≥0 and only touches the axis at one point, revolving it produces a solid, sealed shape rather than a torus with a hole—the boundary surface closes up smoothly, giving something like a bell or dome with a flat-ish bottom.

That inner surface would only be glimpsed through the visor slit anyway, so the backface rendering issue is minor and likely masked by the dark slit paint. Maybe I should simplify by switching the helm's construction to a loft using a decagon cross-section instead of a lathe, giving it a more blocky, stylized look.

I'm sketching out loft stations from bottom to crown with varying widths and heights, using flat caps so the tube closes cleanly at top and bottom, and an octagonal section for a low-poly puppet aesthetic. I'm weighing whether the ngon's vertex should point forward or whether a flat front face would work better so the visor slit lands on a flat surface rather than a seam.

I'm double-checking the frame orientation math for the vertical loft path — tracing through the aim/basis construction confirms the normal ends up roughly along -Z and the binormal along -X, which works fine for symmetric sections since width and depth axes stay consistent either way.

With a circle of 10 sides and the phase offset I chose, the vertices land along the ±X axis while flat faces center on ±Z — exactly what I want so the helm's front has a flat face rather than a vertex, which matters for placing a visor slit. Since the transported normal stays constant at -Z along the straight vertical path, that flat face stays aligned to the front throughout, and I can paint the visor slit using a simple z-coordinate threshold check at the front face.

Working out the geometry, I'm placing a narrow horizontal eye slit on the helm: roughly 0.11 wide and 0.02 tall, positioned at the front flat face (z > 0.05) around y ≈ 1.62, matching the helm's base-to-top range of about 1.47 to 1.76. Since paint is applied in model space, this slit will consistently appear on the front of the helm regardless of orientation.

Now I'm designing the crimson plume as a swept tube along a curved catmull path rising from the helm's crown, arcing backward from around y=1.74 up to y=2.04, with a tapering radius that flattens it into a fan-like shape rather than a round tube.

Defining loft stations...

I'll use a box section for that blocky faceted stylization rather than smooth circle, and finish with a small gold cylinder crest-holder at the helm top where the plume roots in.

For helm trim, I'm adding a thin gold torus band rotated into the horizontal plane to sit as a rim, plus gold stud spheres arranged in a ring frame around the helm's circumference.

Checking the math: with a texture around 2048px and total chart area in the single-digit square meters, I get roughly 1-2.5mm per texel, which comfortably resolves a 0.1m-period filigree pattern and a 0.3m griffin decal. For the shield's paint, I'm thinking through the blue field with a gold border, using the extrude's surface coordinates (local x,y per vertex) to detect proximity to the outline edge rather than trying to compute it from model-space position directly.

Instead of guessing edge thresholds, I'll write a small helper that computes the minimum distance from a point to the kite outline's polygon segments, then use that to paint a gold rim near the edges while keeping the interior blue — straightforward and cheap, and I confirm the surface coordinates do get passed through to the paint function for extrudes.

For the shield's visuals, I'm planning a blue field with that gold rim, a dark dent pattern, and a griffin decal on top, plus a central steel boss modeled as a small lathe dome sitting slightly in front of the shield — though I need to make sure the boss and the griffin decal placement don't overlap awkwardly.
